title.title: Recap
title.subtitle: Six things you already know, one new idea: the permissioned vs permissionless spectrum

recap.heading: Recap in key points
recap.subtitle: No teaching here — just the thread that runs from Fundamentals into this course. Each line points back to where you learned it.

items.text: The trust problem: strangers need one record they all believe, without a referee who can cheat or disappear.
A shared ledger of hashed, chained blocks, copied to every participant, makes that record tamper-evident.
Decentralization is about who controls — who can change or censor the record. The shape of the network is a separate question.
Bitcoin was the first permissionless chain: fixed supply, Proof of Work, nobody to ask for permission.
Bitcoin cannot run programs — its scripting is deliberately limited to moving value.
Ethereum added smart contracts, accounts, gas and tokens — a programmable platform.

next: The recurring question: does this problem earn a blockchain?
recap.keyPoint: Everything so far was one platform family — now we compare platforms.

types.title: Types of Blockchain
types.governance: Permissioned = known members agree the rules and can fix mistakes. Permissionless = nobody can be excluded, and nobody can undo.
types.keyPoint: The three types differ in who may read, write and validate — not in the cryptography underneath.

spectrum.heading: Permissionless ↔ Permissioned: one spectrum, not two camps
spectrum.subtitle: Every platform in this course sits somewhere on this line. Placing a project on it starts with two business questions: who is allowed in, and who needs to see what?
spectrum.leftSub: anyone can join, read and validate

gainRight.title: Move right and you gain
items: Privacy — competitors don't see your volumes or prices
Speed — thousands of transactions per second, no mining
Compliance — known identities, auditable roles (KYC, GDPR)
Control — members agree the rules and can correct mistakes

gainLeft.title: Move left and you gain
items: Open access — no gatekeeper; anyone can join or build
Neutrality — no member can be frozen out or removed
Censorship resistance — rules enforced by code and economics
Network effects — shared users, liquidity and tooling

decision.title: Three questions to place your project

items.q: Do you know — and can you legally hold accountable — every participant?
Must some data stay hidden from some participants?
Does the value depend on anyone in the world being able to join?

spectrum.keyPoint: Permissioned vs permissionless is a question of WHO may write — not how fast it is.

usecases.heading: Does this problem earn a blockchain?
usecases.subtitle: The question we will ask of every platform in this course. Fundamentals §3 covered the industries — here is the checklist.

use.title: ✅ Use a blockchain when…
items: Several parties must share one record and none of them is trusted to keep it alone
The record must be tamper-evident and auditable by outsiders
An intermediary adds cost or delay without adding trust
Rules must run automatically, or no participant may be excludable

dontUse.title: ❌ Don't use a blockchain when…
items: One organisation controls every participant — a database is cheaper and faster
All parties already trust a central party — a regulator, a bank, a registry
Data must stay private and move in high volume — public chains expose everything and are slow
The truth lives off-chain — a blockchain cannot verify what it is told (the oracle problem)

usecases.keyPoint: Carry this question into every platform: does this problem earn a blockchain — and if so, which one?

takeaways.title: Section 00 — Key Takeaways
items: Fundamentals gave you one platform family — Bitcoin and Ethereum are both public, permissionless chains
Permissioned ↔ permissionless is one spectrum: the question is who may write and validate, not how fast it runs
Moving towards permissioned trades open access and censorship resistance for privacy, control and compliance
Governance trade-off: known members can agree rules and fix mistakes; permissionless means nobody can be excluded — and nobody can undo
Consortium chains let competing organisations share infrastructure without handing control to any one of them
The recurring question for every platform: does this problem earn a blockchain — and if so, which one?

sorter.heading: Who may write to this ledger?
sorter.subtitle: Drag each card into a bucket — or tap a card, then a bucket. You get feedback instantly. One question decides everything: who is allowed to add entries?
sorter.scoreReview: — Move the red cards and try again.

cards.label: Bitcoin
cards.why: Anyone with a wallet can send, and anyone can run a node or mine — no gatekeeper decides who writes.

cards.label: A bank's core ledger
cards.why: One institution owns and edits it. A single writer needs a well-run database, not a blockchain.

cards.label: Hyperledger consortium
cards.why: Several known organisations write, each with a certificate issued under the consortium rules — permissioned.

cards.label: Ethereum
cards.why: Anyone can deploy a contract or validate by staking ETH — open to the world, like Bitcoin.

cards.label: A company's SAP database
cards.why: An internal system with one owner, shared with nobody who distrusts the company — a database.

cards.label: A CBDC (central bank digital currency)
cards.why: The central bank decides who runs nodes and who may issue. Pilots such as the digital euro use a permissioned ledger — some skip blockchain altogether.

sorter.keyPoint: If one organisation controls every writer, you do not need a blockchain — you need a database.
sorter.wrongHint: Not quite — drag it to another bucket.
